**What's been completed since your last review (Mar 6):**

- ✅ PR template fully filled out (linked above)

**Why I pushed an empty commit today:**

CI was failing because `bikeshed` v6.1.1 requires Python 3.12+, but the repository's workflow was pinned to Python 3.11. After the upstream workflow was updated (to Python 3.14), I needed to push a new commit to re-trigger CI on this PR. I used an empty commit (`git commit --allow-empty`) purely to kick off a new CI run — no spec changes were made. The CI is now running but is currently **awaiting maintainer approval** to execute (as required for PRs from forks).

**Request:**

Could you please approve the CI workflow run so it can execute? And if possible, could you nudge @a-sully and @mkruisselbrink? They were assigned as reviewers on March 2 — it's been 3 weeks with no response. A quick ping from you would go a long way. Happy to provide any additional context they need.

Thanks for your time and guidance throughout this process!

@fergald can someone from your team take a look please?

This seems like a reasonable change, and is certainly what the spec should have said from the beginning, my mistake.
There is of course a slight web-compat risk with a change like this as @saschanaz was alluding to in #181. So while this makes sense from a spec point of view, it would require implementers to agree to take on the risk of making the change as well, and I'm no longer involved in the implementation of any of this. Hence hopefully @fergald and other implementers can hopefully weigh in.
If we are all agreed on then I'm fine with it too. Maybe would be nice to check known usages like in emscripten. cc @jjjalkanen

IIUC, Chromium [currently](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/modules/file_system_access/file_system_underlying_sink.cc;l=107;drc=8abea14deda089834ba142a35e8342014812df55) throws a SyntaxError in this case any of these are `null`. So the compat risk seems quite low for us.

@mingyc
@fergald isn't that throwing conditional upon the value of type? Because otherwise we might as well make these fields required.

I tested this in Chromium and the behavior appears to depend on the execution path rather than being uniform. In particular: - When `type` is present (e.g. "write" / "truncate"), passing `null` for fields like `position`, `size`, or `data` results in failure during internal algorithm validation, producing a `SyntaxError`. - When `type` is omitted, the failure occurs earlier at the WebIDL boundary with a `TypeError` due to the required `type` member being undefined. So the exception is conditional on the presence of `type`, but not in a single consistent rule across all paths. Instead, different validation layers are triggered depending on how the dictionary is shaped. Firefox and Safari do not yet expose `showSaveFilePicker`, so this was only verifiable in Chromium. I’ve filed the corresponding implementation issues for Gecko and WebKit. Screenshot of the test results for reference: This suggests a split between WebIDL-level validation and algorithm-level validation depending on execution path rather than a single unified null-handling rule.

If you always get an exception it's fine, but just from a brief scan of the Chromium code @fergald pointed to I don't think you get an exception when type is "truncate" and position or data is null. Now perhaps that is unlikely enough to not matter in practice, but that would be a new case where we start throwing assuming I'm understanding that correctly from the limited context.

Now perhaps that is unlikely enough to not matter in practice, but that would be a new case where we start throwing assuming I'm understanding that correctly from the limited context. Thank you for the precise pushback. I've retested with isolated writables (fresh stream per test) to avoid state contamination from earlier failures. Results in Chromium: { type: "truncate", position: null } → SyntaxError: truncate requires a size argument { type: "truncate", data: null } → SyntaxError: truncate requires a size argument So Chromium does throw in both cases, but the error is driven by the missing/null size, not by position or data being null those fields appear to be ignored under truncate. The exception fires regardless of what else is in the dict. The remaining compat risk is { type: "write", position: null } which currently passes silently in Chromium. Making position non-nullable would change that to a TypeError at the WebIDL boundary. That is the one case worth implementers explicitly signing off on.

@annevk based on the test results, the one genuine behavior change this PR introduces is { type: "write", position: null } which currently passes silently in Chromium. Should I update the PR description to explicitly call this out rather than saying "consistent with implementations"? Happy to clarify the wording if that helps move things forward.

It's not that simple as `{ type: "truncate", size, position: null }` doesn't throw today either. I'm not really familiar with how people use this API though and whether that's likely to happen in practice.

So this would force people to supply a `position` for `truncate` and a `size` for `seek`? I don't think that's OK.

This would also cause the [examples on MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FileSystemWritableFileStream/write) to start throwing.

Unless I'm misunderstanding things, these have to be optional.

They remain optional. But if you pass them instead of omitting them and use null as value you would get an exception. That means that `{ type: "truncate", size, position: null }` would start throwing, but `{ type: "truncate", size, position: undefined }` would continue not to throw.

(Unfortunately `?` is very attractive and browsers binding implementations are often lenient (we fixed this in WebKit which is why this came up) so people don't realize they could (and should) just rely on `undefined` when designing APIs.)

> Is that what you mean?

Yes, that's no longer the case in WebKit. In WebKit you are now required to use `std::optional<std::optional<T>>` for cases like this.

WebKit has this dictionary as well, but we don't have telemetry.

So the risks are unknown and we have no good way to measure them and the benefit is unclear. Without evidence that this isn't going to break usage of the API, I don't think we should make this clean-up.
I tend to agree. We should add defaulting to null though. And we should be more careful about this going forward. Perhaps something the TAG can pay attention to @jyasskin & @marcoscaceres?
Or requiring extra extattr on Web IDL level, something similar to what I suggested in https://github.com/whatwg/webidl/issues/1485. (See: https://github.com/whatwg/webidl/issues/1565)

@annevk @fergald Thanks, this helps clarify where things stand.

From the thread, I understand the blocker is no longer whether the current IDL is theoretically ideal, but whether changing `null` handling here is worth the web-compat risk.

To tighten up the evidence on current behavior, I re-ran the Chromium cases with a fresh writable stream per test so earlier failures could not affect later results. The relevant outcomes were:

- `{ type: "write", position: null, data: ... }` currently passes
- `{ type: "write", data: null }` throws
- `{ type: "truncate", size: null }` throws
- `{ type: "truncate", position: null }` throws because truncate requires `size`
- `{ type: "truncate", data: null }` throws because truncate requires `size`

So the main behavior change this PR would introduce is the `write + position:null` case.

Given that, would the following be enough to reconsider this PR:
1. a targeted audit of known usages/libraries/examples for `null` being passed here, or
2. implementer confirmation that the compat risk is acceptable despite limited telemetry?

If not, then I think the best next step is probably to close this PR and instead pursue the alternative mentioned in-thread around explicit defaulting to null / future Web IDL guidance, rather than keep this one open without a realistic merge path.

Thanks for filing the telemetry bug. That makes sense, and I agree that measuring whether real-world sites pass explicit `null` values for `size`, `position`, or `data` would help assess the compatibility risk.
For clarity, this PR changes the behavior only when `null` is explicitly provided; omitted optional members remain optional. I’m happy to update the PR or add tests based on the telemetry results.
